title: The Bigfoot hunt is on: Here are 6 places to sight Sasquatch
excerpt: For a creature that’s supposed to be elusive, Bigfoot is everywhere.
content:
For a creature that’s supposed to be elusive, Bigfoot is everywhere.

In this neck of the woods, you don’t have to hike deep into the forest to find him. Bigfoot sells souvenirs, poses among petunias, peers over fences and mingles on Seattle’s waterfront.

The Pacific Northwest has long embraced the legendary cryptid, a creature never scientifically proven but deeply woven into regional folklore. Washington consistently ranks among the states with the most online reported Bigfoot sightings. The state even has a $5 Sasquatch scratch lottery ticket.

Whether you believe in Bigfoot hardly matters anymore. He has wandered out of the wilderness and settled into everyday life.

Here are six places to spot Sasquatch, plus a few bonus sightings along the way.

1. BIGFOOT BARISTA

At Espresso Chalet along Highway 2 in Index, Bigfoot is served with coffee.

For more than 36 years, travelers rounding a bend on the mountain highway have been greeted by a giant wooden Sasquatch standing beside the rustic chalet-style espresso stand.

Visitors can snap selfies with the towering creature, sip Stevens Passquatch lattes, bite into Bigfoot-shaped cookies and climb onto giant concrete footprints to compare shoe sizes.

Owner Mark Klein said the footprints are modeled after “tracks that were very unexplainable” he saw deep in the woods years ago.

The property even has a Hollywood connection. Its old green Quonset hut appeared in the 1987 cult classic “Harry and the Hendersons,” starring John Lithgow as the father of a Seattle family that accidentally hits a friendly Sasquatch with its station wagon and brings him home.

Espresso Chalet isn’t Washington’s only place to pair caffeine with cryptids. BigFoot Java, founded in 2002 by Bigfoot Investment Group, has espresso stands across the state, including locations in Edmonds, Marysville and Everett.

2. DECEPTION PASS GIANT

On Highway 20, just south of the Deception Pass Bridge at the northern tip of Whidbey Island, a 12-foot chainsaw-carved Bigfoot beckons travelers to Squatchy’s gift shop. It took seven people to hoist the 2,000-pound cedar statue into place in May.

Inside, things get even hairier. A 9-foot Bigfoot, crafted by a taxidermist using bear pelts, was modeled after the creature store co-owner Scott Meaker said he encountered while hiking in Yosemite National Park in the late 1970s. He was 17 when he and his cousin spotted what appeared to be a giant, furr, brown biped striding upright through the woods.

The Bigfoot duo are popular selfie stops, while shoppers browse Sasquatch T-shirts, socks and even Bigfoot scat.

Beyond the cryptids, the lodge-style shop offers a few surprises: a robot cotton-candy machine that belts out cheerful tunes while spinning carnival-sized clouds of pink sugar fluff for $1, an impressive selection of saltwater taffy and an upstairs kids zone with couches, cornhole and a microwave for Hot Pockets.

It’s a three-fer: roadside attraction, candy shop and Bigfoot headquarters.

3. SUBURBAN SASQUATCH

Not every local Sasquatch towers over tourists.

One Everett Bigfoot has quietly become a neighborhood celebrity.

The 8-foot plywood silhouette rises above a front yard bursting with flowers in the 7000 block of Beverly Lane. Overhead flies a collection of flags: American, Norwegian, U.S. Marines and POW/MIA.

The unexpected roadside attraction turns heads on the busy residential street. Neighbors use it as a landmark. Visitors slow down. Kids point from car windows. It’s proof that front yards don’t have to be boring.

Nathaniel Lindell built the original Bigfoot while he was in high school during the COVID-19 shutdowns, when canceled activities left him looking for a project. Someone offered him $100 for it.

He sold it.

Then he built three more.

One was bought as a wedding gift. After all, nothing says “happily ever after” quite like a giant plywood Sasquatch.

Lindell, now 24, recently returned home after serving five years as an embassy guard in the Marines and plans to become an electrician.

Maybe his next Bigfoot will come with its own lighting effects.

4. VIRTUAL HUNT

Finding Bigfoot is as easy as buying a ticket.

At Sasquatch Mountain on Seattle’s Pier 57, visitors strap on a virtual reality headset and head deep into Bigfoot country.

The immersive attraction combines motion seats, wind effects, the scent of pine trees and digital wilderness to create the feeling of tracking the elusive creature through dense forests. The ride twists, turns and bounces over rugged terrain as Sasquatch lurks just out of sight.

The ride is family-friendly, with a minimum height requirement of 42 inches. Tickets are $25 for adults and $20 for youth.

Bigfoot sighting guaranteed.

5. MOSSY MYSTERY

Then there’s Mossman in Lake Stevens.

For years, mysterious moss-covered Bigfoot figures have appeared in the woods on Lundeen Parkway along Stevens Creek.

Where had they come from?

Residents speculated. Rumors spread. Theories multiplied.

Eventually, a local woodworker named Steve stepped forward.

“I did it for the kids,” he said.

The figures are constructed from fencing and draped with living moss. One even came with a baby Sasquatch.

Think giant Chia Pets with oversized feet.

Steve tied them to trees so they don’t wander off.

Probably a wise precaution.

6. ART SQUATCH

Bigfoot pops up in plenty of other unexpected places.

The Schack Art Center in Everett has Schacksquatch, three 18-foot public sculptures by Tulalip Tribes artist James Madison. Inspired by Coast Salish storytelling traditions, the works honor Indigenous culture while reflecting the enduring presence of Sasquatch in Pacific Northwest lore.

The Skagit-Squatch Museum, 516 Avon Ave. in Burlington, has more than 600 paintings, sculptures and anything you can imagine Bigfoot. Outside, carved wooden creatures cover the quirky building, inspiring an immediate “Did I really just see that?” double take.

Artist Ryan Henry Ward, known simply as “Henry,” took the region’s Bigfoot fascination a step further.

He surpassed his goal to paint 1,000 of his whimsical Sassy Sasquatches across Washington. About 1,500 property owners volunteered their fences, garages, homes and businesses.

The wide-eyed, goofy Sasquatches appear on everything from million-dollar homes to single-wide trailers. Part of the fun is spotting them because there’s no official map.

Like Bigfoot himself, they tend to appear when you least expect them.

Hint: There’s one painted on a fence along the south side of Madison Street, just east of Evergreen Way in Everett.

WEST VS. EAST BIGFOOT

Theories vary by region.

West Coast sightings typically describe massive creatures slipping silently through dense forests.

Reports from the eastern United States often feature smaller beings, glowing eyes, strange odors and other unexplained details.

Florida even has its own version: the Skunk Ape.

Some believers insist these are different species. Skeptics argue that every region simply invents the monster that best fits its landscape.

But nowhere seems to have embraced Bigfoot quite like the Pacific Northwest.

Whatever the truth, Bigfoot has become more than a campfire legend.

You can buy his socks.

Drink his coffee.

Eat his cookies.

Pose beside him for a selfie.

Spot him in a flower garden.

Or encounter him at Deception Pass after a robot spins you cotton candy.

For a creature no one has proved exists, Bigfoot has built an impressive résumé: barista, lawn ornament, mural muse and virtual-reality star.

Not bad for someone who’s supposed to be hiding.
